extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy and law; readers of Montesquieu
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Montesquieu's normative and explanatory principles about government, commerce, colonies, credit, civil society, and especially tolerance in matters of religion, as presented with editorial notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Island commercial nation tends to be non-conquerant
rubrics_metrics.description: If a nation inhabited an island and prospered by commerce, it would not be naturally conquerant: separate conquests would weaken it; fertile soil would further reduce need for war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu argues that geographic/island setting + commercial prosperity produce incentives toward peace rather than conquest, because the costs of separate conquests and lack of need to enrich by war reduce expansionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public credit and internal borrowing strengthen liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation that borrows from itself (internal public credit) pays and borrows to itself and thus would have secure credit; subjects would have an interest in defending the nation's liberty because their loans and credit depend on its independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial note: public/internal debt can create a stake for citizens in defending the state; Montesquieu sees this as a mechanism that ties private interest to public defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial nations develop many private interests and jealousies
rubrics_metrics.description: A commercial nation has a prodigious number of small private interests, making it liable to be offended or to offend in an infinity of ways; such nations become supremely jealous and may grieve more over others' prosperity than enjoy their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for policy: commercial complexity creates domestic factionalism and external rivalry; trade policy and navigation laws may thus be both gentle in general but rigidly protective in commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval supremacy follows from island commerce and absence of land forces
rubrics_metrics.description: A dominant commercial island lacking fortresses and land armies must rely on a powerful navy to preserve liberty from invasion; consequently its marine will exceed that of land-focused powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu links constitutional/needing-to-defend-liberty to choice of military investments: maritime strength over land forces when colonies and commerce predominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies tend to adopt mother country's government and become dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: When a nation sends colonies it will give them its own form of government; although colonized peoples may prosper under that government, the colony can remain economically/legally dependent so that the conquered state is free in form but the overarching polity remains master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: colonization often extends institutions and prosperity but can create lasting dependency enforced by laws of nations and unequal treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers accountable to popular councils are constrained to probity
rubrics_metrics.description: If ministers must justify their conduct before a popular council, their negotiations cannot be secret and they will be forced to greater honesty and probity in diplomacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu suggests institutional transparency (ministerial accountability) promotes public probity in foreign affairs and reduces secretive misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where nobles are reduced and people elevated, forms of absolute power may persist in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if nobles have been abased and the people elevated, remnants or forms of arbitrary power from prior despotism may persist as styles on a nominally free government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: legal or ceremonial survivals of earlier absolutism can coexist with a free constitutional structure, producing hybrid or deceptive appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: When laws permit several religions, they must require mutual tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the laws of a State allow several religions, they must also oblige them to tolerate one another; a citizen must not only abstain from disturbing the State but also must not trouble any fellow citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental political principle: plural legal recognition of religions should be paired with legal obligations of inter-confessional non-interference to prevent cycles of repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: A repressed religion becomes repressive when freed
rubrics_metrics.description: Any religion which is repressed becomes itself repressive: once liberated from oppression it will attack the religion that repressed it, not as religion but as tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu asserts a predictable cycle: repression breeds counter-repression when power shifts; laws should account for this dynamic to prevent future persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: State choice about admitting new religions — do not establish new ones; tolerate established ones
rubrics_metrics.description: When a State is master to receive a new religion or not, it should not establish it; but when a religion is already established, it must be tolerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle for religious policy: the sovereign decision to admit new cults should err on non-establishment, and once a religion is entrenched legal tolerance becomes a political necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing the dominant religion by sovereign decree is highly risky
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince who sets out to destroy or change the dominant religion in his State exposes himself to great danger; in despotic governments the risk of revolution from imposed religious change is particularly high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: abrupt top-down religious reform clashes with entrenched social practices, constitutionally-linked institutions, and popular attachment; gradual persuasion is safer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid penal laws in matters of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: One should avoid penal laws regarding religion: though they inspire fear, because religion itself has fearful penalties/promises, civil penalties and religious sanctions counteract and brutalize souls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu's rule: penal measures against conscience are counterproductive and morally corrosive; civil policy should prefer non-coercive measures in matters of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incentives over penalties to change religious adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: In matters of changing religion, invitations (favours, conveniences, hope of fortune) are stronger than punishments; one should attack religion by offering benefits, not by threatening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: persuasion by improvement of material conditions and civil incentives succeeds better than coercion; historical examples (e.g., persecutions in Japan) support this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persecutions provoke revolt more than long predictable penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: History shows that cruel persecutions create violent revolt, whereas long, drawn-out penalties tend to wear people down; therefore extreme coercion is more likely to produce backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical note from history: visible cruelty mobilizes resistance; longer, less spectacular penalties may be less likely to spark immediate insurrection but are still problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy without coercive force will rely on persuasion and produce learned writings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the clergy lack coercive protection from the State, they will seek to persuade rather than compel and will produce excellent writings to defend revelation and providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: a tolerant civil order reshapes clerical strategies toward intellectual and moral persuasion rather than legal compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: If clergy are allowed to self-govern without oversight, public may refuse to allow them to correct their own abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: It could happen that assemblies are eluded and the public will not permit clergy to correct their own abuses; by a frenzy for liberty people may prefer an imperfect reform to clerical reformation backed by coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: unchecked clerical autonomy combined with public distrust produces stalemate where neither reform nor correction is permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom values reasoning regardless of correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: In a free nation it is often indifferent whether individuals reason well or badly; it suffices that they reason — freedom guarantees the effects of those reasonings rather than their correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual principle about political culture: freedom privileges the activity of public reasoning and debate over the epistemic quality of each individual's arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians lie under both absolute and extreme liberty but for different reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: In extremely absolute monarchies historians betray truth because they lack freedom to speak; in extremely free states they betray truth because their factional prejudices make each slave to their party's views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: both repression and uncontrolled factionalism distort historical truth; institutional balance is needed for reliable historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness arises from leisure; absolute governments create the leisure that breeds certain politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The politeness of manners depends on leisure and is more prevalent when governments produce conditions of idleness (as with absolute power); more people needing social niceties generates more politeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociological observation: cultural refinements (politeness of manners) have material and institutional causes; they are not purely moral achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire in free societies tends to be harsher and more severe
rubrics_metrics.description: In societies of retreat and solitary thought, satirical writings will be bloodier; free nations produce sharper satirists (many Juvénals before Horaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary consequence: freedom encourages uncompromising critique and harsh satire; refinement of taste may follow later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws are human reason intended to substitute reason for force and to promote peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The law in general is human reason: laws aim to substitute rule by reason for brute force, to foresee conflicts and regulate them according to justice and common interest; peace, not war, should be the guiding end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative axiom: legislation should be grounded in rational anticipation of conflicts and oriented toward public peace and mutual interest rather than coercive domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: No one best government — government must fit the people's disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The government most conformable to nature is the one that best relates to the disposition of the people for which it is established; there is not a single best type of government applicable everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: constitutional and institutional forms must be adapted to social, geographic, and cultural conditions rather than imposed as universal models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: nature of a government vs its principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu distinguishes the nature of a government (what makes it exist) and its principle (what makes it act); the former is structure, the latter the passions that move it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical tool: when evaluating a regime, consider both its structural composition and the motivating principles (ambition, honor, fear, etc.) that animate political behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three species of good government (classical typology)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three fundamental species of government — one, several, or many in authority — which (when aiming at the public good) correspond to monarchy (one), aristocracy (several), and republic/democracy (many). When vitiated they become tyranny, oligarchy, and demagogy respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomy: use this tripartite classification to analyze regimes; judge them by whether authority is exercised for common good or private advantage.
